title: HTML Formatting: Parsing, Whitespace, and Safety Limits
description: What the HTML formatter, minifier, entity encoder and decoder each change, why head and doctype vanish, why minify ruins pre, and when output is not safe HTML.
content:
An HTML formatter hands a piece of source code to the browser's HTML parser, then walks the nodes inside body and writes them back out with two-space indentation. The same tool can also squeeze code onto a single line, turn special characters into entities, and turn entities back into text. The first three actions all parse first and then walk the tree; entity encoding only does string replacement — and that difference decides what it actually changes.

Three buttons parse first; entity encoding only does replacement

Format, minify and decode all enter through new DOMParser().parseFromString(输入, 'text/html'): parse the string into a document tree first, then walk the tree and reassemble a string. Entity encoding takes the other route, making four replacements directly on the input string without ever parsing.

  • Format: walk down level by level from doc.body.childNodes, two spaces of indentation per level; when an element holds only text children, its textContent is trimmed and placed as-is into a single array entry (internal newlines and spaces are not collapsed); text nodes under a mixed-content element have runs of whitespace collapsed to a single space; the walk handles only text nodes and element nodes, so comments are skipped; the 13 void elements area, base, br, col, embed, hr, img, input, link, meta, source, track, wbr emit only a start tag, and every attribute is given double quotes, with a double quote inside the value turned into ".
  • Minify: the same parse and the same walk, but no newlines or indentation are emitted, and runs of whitespace in every text node are replaced with a single space.
  • Encode entities: exactly four replacements, in the order &, <, >, ". The ampersand goes first so that the entities the tool itself produces are not escaped a second time.
  • Decode entities: after parsing it reads doc.body.textContent, which amounts to stripping every tag and then decoding one layer of entities.

Once this is clear, every symptom later in the article follows from it: the tool works on the parsed document, not on the source you typed.

What formatting changes

Format a complete document that has a doctype and a head, and only the contents of body come back: the doctype, title and meta all vanish, because the walk starts at doc.body. Run this step in a real browser with the full document in the input box, and the output box is left with only the elements div, h2 and p.

A few common changes, with every string below taken from measured output:

InputAfter formattingWhy
<!DOCTYPE html>…<head><title>页面标题</title></head>…only <div><p>… is leftthe walk starts at body
<!--keep me-->the comment disappearsonly text and element nodes are handled
<table><tr><td>1</td><td>2</td></tr></table>an extra <tbody> layer appearsthe HTML parser completes the table structure
<p>a<b>x</b>y</p>split across seven lines, renders as a x ythe inline element lands on its own lines, and each new line counts as one space
<pre>if (a) {<span>return b;</span>}</pre>the span gets a line to itselfmixed content inside preformatted text is re-wrapped

The last two rows are where people trip up. When rendered, a newline between inline elements counts as one space, so after the compact <p>a<b>x</b>y</p> is formatted, the text on the page goes from axy to a x y; when pre holds a mix of elements, the text portion is trimmed onto its own line and the original indentation shifts along with it.

The price of minifying

Minify replaces the runs of whitespace in every text node with a single space without looking at the ancestor, so preformatted content is the first casualty: <pre>line1 plus a newline and indentation followed by line2</pre> becomes <pre>line1 line2</pre>, and newlines inside textarea are eaten the same way. Ordinary paragraphs show no difference; for a code sample it is a layout accident.

Attributes are the subtler case. Formatting converts a double quote inside an attribute value into an entity; minifying does not: <div title='a"b'>x</div> minifies to <div title="a"b">x</div>, and once the browser parses that, the attribute splits into title="a" and an empty attribute named b" (written b"="" in outerHTML), which changes the meaning outright.

Encoding and decoding entities

Encoding touches only four characters: &, <, >, ". Because & is replaced first, a single pass does not nest inside itself; but if the content you paste is already encoded, one more click yields double escapes such as &amp; (shown on the page as &). Single quotes are outside its scope, so watch for them when you write into a value wrapped in single quotes.

Decoding is more of a purification step: it parses first and then reads textContent, so tags are stripped. Given <p>Hello <b>world</b> & <i>all</i></p> the result is Hello world & all, with both b and i gone; and it unwraps only one layer, so &lt;script&gt; yields the text <script> and does not go on to become a tag. To decode repeatedly you have to click repeatedly.

Boundaries and limits: formatting is not sanitizing

Formatted output never re-escapes text nodes. The safe input <script>alert(1)</script> comes back as a real <script> tag, because the contents of the text node are written out verbatim.

The tool itself does not execute it: the result goes into textarea.value and takes no part in page parsing. In a measured run, inserting that output into a blank page with innerHTML turns up 1 script element, but the script does not run; save this kind of output as an .html file and open it in a browser, and the script runs. The difference is not in the tool but in whether you treat the output as text or as HTML.

Another counterintuitive point: the tool's “HTML parse failed” branch almost never fires. text/html goes through the error-tolerant parser, so broken tags are repaired rather than reported, and MDN also notes that parsererror is tied to XML parse failures. For <div><p>unclosed <span>x</div> the status still reads formatting complete, and the output is repaired into three levels, div, p and span.

The same trap appears in other contexts: writing the output into an attribute value, splicing it into a template string, or handing it to a framework's innerHTML binding all make the characters you escaped take effect again. To display code, put it in pre and encode entities; to generate a page, let a template engine or a sanitizing library handle it.

Nor is it a general-purpose formatter: it does not preserve whitespace semantics, does not keep the compact inline form (inline elements are split across lines), does not understand template syntax (Vue directives or JSX attribute expressions are treated as ordinary attributes), and does not sanitize at all. To tidy source code to an engineering standard, hand it to a tool such as prettier.

How to confirm formatting did not change the page

Before formatted code goes into production, run three checks; they are more reliable than reading it over by eye:

  1. Compare the rendered text: parse the input and the output separately with new DOMParser().parseFromString(文本, 'text/html'), read body.textContent, and collapse runs of whitespace to a single space. The two sides should match. The earlier a<b>x</b>y example fails right here: the input is axy, the output is a x y.
  2. Compare structure counts: count script, style, pre and table elements. A mismatch usually means some text was read as a tag, or that the parser added a structural layer.
  3. Check the delta in dangerous nodes: extra script tags or event attributes beginning with on in the output mean escaping was lost during formatting, and that output cannot go into a page as it is.

Passing all three only proves that the text and the structure did not change; content that never enters body, such as the doctype, head and comments, needs a separate check.

When to use it, and when not to

  • Good for: quickly seeing the hierarchy of a piece of HTML; minifying template fragments you control that contain no pre or textarea; converting a small piece of text into entities.
  • Avoid: rendering user-submitted HTML straight after formatting it, since escaping is lost in the output and that amounts to skipping sanitizing; minifying a whole page, where the whitespace in pre and textarea gets eaten; formatting an entire document and then overwriting the source file, where head and doctype disappear.

It is a layout tool more than a compiler: it works on the tree and does not preserve your formatting intent for the source. The safest habit is to decide first whether you want text or HTML: for a page to display, encode; for an editor to read, format; for a build, confirm first that the fragment contains no pre or textarea.

For stylesheets and scripts use the CSS formatter and the JavaScript formatter; when you want to confirm exactly which characters changed, the text diff is more direct. You can also open the HTML formatter and reproduce each example above.

faqs.a: The structure usually survives, but whitespace semantics, comments and head all change: the doctype, title and meta of a full document never appear in the output, comments are dropped, and inline elements split across lines render with extra spaces. Diff against the source file before you overwrite it.

faqs.q: Why do head and doctype disappear from the output?
faqs.a: After parsing, the tool walks from doc.body, and the title, meta and style inside head sit outside that range. It is meant to re-indent fragments of body, not to tidy a whole document.

faqs.q: Does minifying change how the page renders?
faqs.a: Not for ordinary paragraphs, because runs of whitespace are merged when HTML renders anyway. But pre and textarea depend on literal newlines, and minifying collapses them into spaces, so code samples and prefilled text get distorted.

faqs.q: Is the tool safe for HTML that contains scripts?
faqs.a: The tool itself only writes the result into a text box and does not execute scripts. But the output is not re-escaped, so a previously safe <script> turns back into a real tag; inserting that output into a page, or saving it as a page, carries execution risk, and you must escape or filter it yourself before rendering.

sources.title: WHATWG HTML Standard: parsing HTML documents

focus: Parse first, then serialize: formatting walks from body, minify collapses whitespace, entity decoding strips tags and does not re-escape.
notice: The tool runs locally in your browser, so nothing is uploaded; it does not sanitize, so you must escape or filter the output yourself before rendering or saving it as a page.
